entries.74bfbe2f2f51239aa61387dd423a9178c923ae61: <div sID="gen17322" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Jer.7" sID="Jer.7"/> <div eID="gen17322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17323" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17324" type="x-p"/> The prophet having in God's name reproved the people for their sins, and given them warning of the judgments of God that were coming upon them, in this chapter prosecutes the same intention for their humiliation and awakening. I. He shows them the invalidity of the plea they so much relied on, that they had the temple of God among them and constantly attended the service of it, and endeavours to take them off from their confidence in their external privileges and performances, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.1-Jer.7.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. He reminds them of the desolations of Shiloh, and foretels that such should be the desolations of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.12-Jer.7.16">ver. 12-16</reference>. III. He represents to the prophet their abominable idolatries, for which he was thus incensed against them, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.17-Jer.7.20">ver. 17-20</reference>. IV. He sets before the people that fundamental maxim of religion that "to obey is better than sacrifice" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1 Sam. xv. 22</reference>), and that God would not accept the sacrifices of those that obstinately persisted in disobedience, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.21-Jer.7.28">ver. 21-28</reference>. V. He threatens to lay the land utterly waste for their idolatry and impiety, and to multiply their slain as they had multiplied their sin, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.29-Jer.7.34">ver. 29-34</reference>.
entries.13a6b425f06bdd0b9987bbb7c092cd5f8b07e10d: <div eID="gen17324" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17323" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">A Call of Repentance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17325" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word that came to Jeremiah from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Stand in the gate of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house, and proclaim there this word, and say, Hear the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all <hi type="italic">ye of</hi> Judah, that enter in at these gates to worship the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">3</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel, Amend your ways and your doings, and I will cause you to dwell in this place. <hi type="super">4</hi> Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , The temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , The temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">are</hi> these. <hi type="super">5</hi> For if ye throughly amend your ways and your doings; if ye throughly execute judgment between a man and his neighbour; <hi type="super">6</hi> <hi type="italic">If</hi> ye oppress not the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, and shed not innocent blood in this place, neither walk after other gods to your hurt: <hi type="super">7</hi> Then will I cause you to dwell in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers, for ever and ever. <hi type="super">8</hi> Behold, ye trust in lying words, that cannot profit. <hi type="super">9</hi> Will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery, and swear falsely, and burn incense unto Baal, and walk after other gods whom ye know not; <hi type="super">10</hi> And come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, We are delivered to do all these abominations? <hi type="super">11</hi> Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, even I have seen <hi type="italic">it,</hi> saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">12</hi> But go ye now unto my place which <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Shiloh, where I set my name at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel. <hi type="super">13</hi> And now, because ye have done all these works, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and I spake unto you, rising up early and speaking, but ye heard not; and I called you, but ye answered not; <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore will I do unto <hi type="italic">this</hi> house, which is called by my name, wherein ye trust, and unto the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I have done to Shiloh. <hi type="super">15</hi> And I will cast you out of my sight, as I have cast out all your brethren, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the whole seed of Ephraim. <div eID="gen17325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17326" type="x-p"/> These verses begin another sermon, which is continued in this and the two following chapters, much to the same effect with those before, to reason them to repentance. Observe, <div eID="gen17326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17327" type="x-p"/> I. The orders given to the prophet to preach this sermon; for he had not only a general commission, but particular directions and instructions for every message he delivered. This was <hi type="italic">a word</hi> that <hi type="italic">came to him from the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.7.1">v. 1</reference>. We are not told when this sermon was to be preached; but are told, 1. Where it must be preached—<hi type="italic">in the gate of the Lord's house,</hi> through which they entered into the outer court, or the <hi type="italic">court of the people.</hi> It would affront the priests, and expose the prophet to their rage, to have such a message as this delivered within their precincts; but the prophet must not fear the face of man, he cannot be faithful to his God if he do. 2. To whom it must be preached—to the men of <hi type="italic">Judah, that enter in at these gates to worship the Lord;</hi> probably it was at one of three feasts, when all the males from all parts of the country were to appear before the Lord in the courts of his house, and not to <hi type="italic">appear empty:</hi> then he had many together to preach to, and that was the most seasonable time to admonish them not to trust to their privileges. Note, (1.) Even those that profess religion have need to be preached to as well as those that are without. (2.) It is desirable to have opportunity of preaching to many together. Wisdom chooses to cry <hi type="italic">in the chief place of concourse,</hi> and, as Jeremiah here, <hi type="italic">in the opening of the gates,</hi> the temple-gates. (3.) When we are going to worship God we have need to be admonished to <hi type="italic">worship him in the spirit,</hi> and <hi type="italic">to have no confidence in the flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.3">Phil. iii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen17327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17328" type="x-p"/> II. The contents and scope of the sermon itself. It is delivered in the name of <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel,</hi> who commands the world, but covenants with his people. As creatures we are bound to regard the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts,</hi> as Christians <hi type="italic">the God of Israel;</hi> what he said to them he says to us, and it is much the same with that which John Baptist said to those whom he baptized (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.8-Matt.3.9">Matt. iii. 8, 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Bring forth fruits meet for repentance; and think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father.</hi> The prophet here tells them, <div eID="gen17328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17329" type="x-p"/> 1. What were the true words of God, which they might trust to. In short, they might depend upon it that if they would repent and reform their lives, and return to God in a way of duty, he would restore and confirm their peace, would redress their grievances, and return to them in a way of mercy (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Amend your ways and your doings.</hi> This implies that there had been much amiss in their ways and doings, many faults and errors. But it is a great instance of the favour of God to them that he gives them liberty to amend, shows them where and how they must amend, and promises to accept them upon their amendment: "<hi type="italic">I will cause you to dwell</hi> quietly and peaceably <hi type="italic">in this place,</hi> and a stop shall be put to that which threatens your expulsion." Reformation is the only way, and a sure way to ruin. He explains himself (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.5-Jer.7.7">v. 5-7</reference>), and tells them particularly, <div eID="gen17329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17330" type="x-p"/> (1.) What the amendment was which he expected from them. They must <hi type="italic">thoroughly amend;</hi> in <hi type="italic">making good,</hi> they must <hi type="italic">make good their ways and doings;</hi> they must reform with resolution, and it must be a universal, constant, preserving reformation—not partial, but entire—not hypocritical, but sincere—not wavering, but constant. They must make the tree good, and so make the fruit good, must amend their hearts and thoughts, and so amend their ways and doings. In particular, [1.] They must be honest and just in all their dealings. Those that had power in their hands must <hi type="italic">thoroughly execute judgment between a man and his neighbour,</hi> without partiality, and according as the merits of the cause appeared. They must not either in judgment or in contract <hi type="italic">oppress the stranger, the fatherless, or the widow,</hi> nor countenance or protect those that did oppress, nor refuse to do them justice when they sought for it. They must <hi type="italic">not shed innocent blood,</hi> and with it defile <hi type="italic">this place</hi> and the land wherein they dwelt. [2.] They must keep closely to the worship of the true God only: "<hi type="italic">Neither walk after other gods;</hi> do not hanker after them, nor hearken to those that would draw you into communion with idolaters; for it is, and will be, <hi type="italic">to your own hurt.</hi> Be not only so just to your God, but so wise for yourselves, as not to throw away your adorations upon those who are not able to help you, and thereby provoke him who is able to destroy you." Well, this is all that God insists upon. <div eID="gen17330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17331" type="x-p"/> (2.) He tells them what the establishment is which, upon this amendment, they may expect from him (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.7">v. 7</reference>): "Set about such a work of reformation as this with all speed, go through with it, and abide by it; <hi type="italic">and I will cause you to dwell in this place,</hi> this temple; it shall continue your place of resort and refuge, the place of your comfortable meeting with God and one another; and you shall dwell <hi type="italic">in the land that I gave to your fathers for ever and ever,</hi> and it shall never be turned out either from God's house or from your own." It is promised that they shall still enjoy their civil and sacred privileges, that they shall have a comfortable enjoyment of them: <hi type="italic">I will cause you to dwell here;</hi> and those dwell at ease to whom God gives a settlement. They shall enjoy it by covenant, by virtue of the grant made of it to their fathers, not by providence, but by promise. They shall continue in the enjoyment of it without eviction or molestation; they shall not be disturbed, much less dispossessed, <hi type="italic">for ever and ever;</hi> nothing but sin could throw them out. An everlasting inheritance in the heavenly Canaan is hereby secured to all that live in godliness and honesty. And the vulgar Latin reads a further privilege here, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.3">v. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.7">7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Habitabo vobiscum—I will dwell with you in this place;</hi> and we should find Canaan itself but an uncomfortable place to dwell in if God did not dwell with us there. <div eID="gen17331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17332" type="x-p"/> 2. What were the lying words of their own hearts, which they must not trust to. He cautions them against this self-deceit (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Trust not in lying words.</hi> You are told in what way, and upon what terms, you may be easy safe, and happy; now do not flatter yourselves with an opinion that you may be so on any other terms, or in any other way." Yet he charges them with this self-deceit arising from vanity (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Behold,</hi> it is plain that <hi type="italic">you</hi> do <hi type="italic">trust in lying words,</hi> notwithstanding what is said to you; you trust in <hi type="italic">words that cannot profit;</hi> you rely upon a plea that will stand you in no stead." Those that slight the words of truth, which would profit them, take shelter in words of falsehood, which cannot profit them. Now these lying words were, "<hi type="italic">The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord are these.</hi> These buildings, the courts, the holy place, and the holy of holies, are the <hi type="italic">temple of the Lord,</hi> built by his appointment, to his glory; here he resides, here he is worshipped, here we meet three times a year to pay our homage to him as our King in his palace." This they thought was security enough to them to keep God and his favours from leaving them, God and his judgments from breaking in upon them. When the prophets told them how sinful they were, and how miserable they were likely to be, still they appealed to the temple: "How can we be either so or so, as long as we have that holy happy place among us?" The prophet repeats it because they repeated it upon all occasions. It was the cant of the times; it was in their mouths upon all occasions. If they heard an awakening sermon, if any startling piece of news was brought to them, they lulled themselves asleep again with this, "We cannot but do well, for we have <hi type="italic">the temple of the Lord among us.</hi>" Note, The privileges of a <hi type="italic">form of godliness</hi> are often the pride and confidence of those that are strangers and enemies to the power of it. It is common for those that are furthest from God to boast themselves most of their being near to the church. They are <hi type="italic">haughty because of the holy mountain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.11">Zeph. iii. 11</reference>), as if God's mercy were so tied to them that they might defy his justice. Now to convince them what a frivolous plea this was, and what little stead it would stand them in, <div eID="gen17332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17333" type="x-p"/> (1.) He shows them the gross absurdity of it in itself. If they knew any thing either of the <hi type="italic">temple of the Lord</hi> or of the <hi type="italic">Lord of the temple,</hi> they must think that to plead that, either in excuse of their sin against God or in arrest of God's judgment against them, was the most ridiculous unreasonable thing that could be. [1.] God is a holy God; but this plea made him the patron of sin, of the worst of sins, which even the light of nature condemns, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.9-Jer.7.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. "What," says he, "<hi type="italic">will you steal, murder, and commit adultery,</hi> be guilty of the vilest immoralities, and which the common interest, as well as the common sense, of mankind witness against? <hi type="italic">Will you swear falsely,</hi> a crime which all nations (who with the belief of a God have had a veneration for an oath) have always had a horror of? Will <hi type="italic">you burn incense to Baal,</hi> a dunghill-deity, that sets up as a rival with the great Jehovah, and, not content with that, <hi type="italic">will you walk after other gods</hi> too, <hi type="italic">whom you know not,</hi> and by all these crimes put a daring affront upon God, both as <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts</hi> and as the <hi type="italic">God of Israel?</hi> Will you exchange a God of whose power and goodness you have had such a long experience for gods of whose ability and willingness to help you you know nothing? And, when you have thus done the worst you can against God, will you brazen your faces so far as to come and <hi type="italic">stand before him in this house which is called by his name</hi> and in which his name is called upon—stand before him as servants waiting his commands, as supplicants expecting his favour? Will you act in open rebellion against him, and yet herd among his subjects, among the best of them? By this, it should seem, you think that either he does not discover or does not dislike your wicked practices, to imagine either of which is to put the highest indignity possible upon him. It is as if you should say, <hi type="italic">We are delivered to do all these abominations.</hi>" If they had not the front to say this, <hi type="italic">totidem verbis—in so many words,</hi> yet their actions spoke it aloud. They could not but own that God, even their own God, had many a time delivered them, and been a present help to them, when otherwise they must have perished. He, in delivering them, designed to reduce them to himself, and by his goodness to lead them to repentance; but they resolved to persist in their abominations notwithstanding. As soon as they were delivered (as of old in the days of the Judges) they <hi type="italic">did evil again in the sight of the Lord,</hi> which was in effect to say, in direct contradiction to the true intent and meaning of the providences which had affected them, that God had delivered them in order to put them again into a capacity of rebelling against him, by sacrificing the more profusely to their idols. Note, Those who continue in sin because grace has abounded, or that grace may abound, do in effect make Christ the minister of sin. Some take it thus: "You present yourselves before God with your sacrifices and sin-offerings, and then say, <hi type="italic">We are delivered,</hi> we are discharged from our guilt, now it shall do us no hurt; when all this is but to blind the world, and stop the mouth of conscience, that you may, the more easily to yourselves and the more plausibly before others, <hi type="italic">do all these abominations.</hi>" [2.] His temple was a holy place; but this plea made it a protection to the most unholy persons: "<hi type="italic">Has this house, which is called by my name</hi> and is a standing sign of God's kingdom of sin and Satan—<hi type="italic">has this become a den of robbers in your eyes?</hi> Do you think it was built to be not only a rendezvous of, but a refuge and shelter to, the vilest of malefactors?" No; though the horns of the altar were a sanctuary to him that slew a man unawares, yet they were not so to a wilful murderer, nor to one that did aught presumptuously, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.14">Exod. xxi. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.29">1 Kings ii. 29</reference>. Those that think to excuse themselves in unchristian practices with the Christian name, and sin the more boldly and securely because there is a sin-offering provided, do, in effect, make God's house of prayer a den of thieves, as the priests in Christ's time, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.13">Matt. xxi. 13</reference>. But could they thus impose upon God? No: <hi type="italic">Behold, I have seen it, saith the Lord,</hi> have seen the real iniquity through the counterfeit and dissembled piety. Note, Though men may deceive one another with the appearances of devotion, yet they cannot deceive God. <div eID="gen17333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17334" type="x-p"/> (2.) He shows them the insufficiency of this plea adjudged long since in the case of Shiloh. [1.] It is certain that Shiloh was ruined, though it had God's sanctuary in it, when by its wickedness it profaned that sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Go you now to my place which was in Shiloh.</hi> It is probable that the ruins of that once flourishing city were yet remaining; they might, at least, read the history of it, which ought to affect them as if they saw the place. There God <hi type="italic">set his name at the first,</hi> there the tabernacle was set up when Israel first took possession of Canaan (<reference osisRef="John.18.1">John xviii. 1</reference>), and thither the tribes went up; but those that attended the service of the tabernacle there corrupted both themselves and others, and from them arose the <hi type="italic">wickedness of his people Israel;</hi> that fountain was poisoned, and sent forth malignant streams; and what came of it? No; God <hi type="italic">forsook</hi> it (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.60">Ps. lxxviii. 60</reference>), sent his ark into captivity, cut off the house of Eli that presided there; and it is very probable that the city was quite destroyed, for we never read any more of it but as a monument of divine vengeance upon holy places when they harbour wicked people. Note, God's judgments upon others, who have really revolted from God while they have kept up a profession of nearness to him, should be a warning to us not to <hi type="italic">trust in lying words.</hi> It is good to consult precedents, and make use of them. <hi type="italic">Remember Lot's wife;</hi> remember Shiloh and the seven churches of Asia; and know that the ark and candlestick are moveable things, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.5">Rev. ii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.43">Matt. xxi. 43</reference>. [2.] It is as certain that Shiloh's fate will be Jerusalem's doom if a speedy and sincere repentance prevent it not. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Jerusalem was now as sinful as ever Shiloh was; that is proved by the unerring testimony of God himself against them (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You have done all these works,</hi> you cannot deny it:" and they continued obstinate in their sin; that is proved by the testimony of God's return and repent, <hi type="italic">rising up early and speaking,</hi> as one in care, as one in earnest, as one who would lose no time in dealing with them, nay, who would take the fittest opportunity for speaking to them early <hi type="italic">in the morning,</hi> when, if ever, they were sober, and had their thoughts free and clear; but it was all in vain. God spoke, but they <hi type="italic">heard not,</hi> they heeded not, they never minded; he <hi type="italic">called them,</hi> but they <hi type="italic">answered not;</hi> they would not come at his call. Note, What God has spoken to us greatly aggravates what we have done against him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Jerusalem shall shortly be as miserable as ever Shiloh was: <hi type="italic">Therefore I will do unto this house as I did to Shiloh,</hi> ruin it, and lay it waste, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.14">v. 14</reference>. Those that tread in the steps of the wickedness of those that went before them must expect to fall by the like judgments, for all these things <hi type="italic">happened to them for ensamples.</hi> The temple at Jerusalem, though ever so strongly built, if wickedness was found in it, would be as unable to keep its ground and as easily conquered as even the tabernacle in Shiloh was, when God's day of vengeance had come. "This house" (says God) "is <hi type="italic">called by my name,</hi> and therefore you may think that I should protect it; it is the house <hi type="italic">in which you trust,</hi> and you think that it will protect you; this land is <hi type="italic">the place,</hi> this city <hi type="italic">the place, which I gave to you and your fathers,</hi> and therefore you are secure of the continuance of it, and think that nothing can turn you out of it; but the men of Shiloh thus flattered themselves and did but deceive themselves." He quotes another precedent (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.15">v. 15</reference>), the ruin of the kingdom of the ten tribes, who were the seed of Abraham, and had the covenant of circumcision, and possessed the land which God gave to them and their fathers, and yet the idolatries threw them out and extirpated them: "And can you think but that the same evil courses will be as fatal to you?" Doubtless they will be so; for God is uniform and of a piece with himself in his judicial proceedings. It is a rule of justice, <hi type="italic">ut parium par sit ratio—that in similar cases the same judgment should proceed.</hi> "You have corrupted <hi type="italic">yourselves as your brethren</hi> the <hi type="italic">seed of Ephraim</hi> did, and have become their brethren in iniquity, and therefore I will <hi type="italic">cast you out of my sight, as I have cast them.</hi>" The interpretation here given of the judgment makes it a terrible one indeed; the casting of them out of their land signified God's casting them out of his sight, as if he would never look upon them, never look after them, more. Whenever we are cast, it is well enough, if we be kept in the love of God; but, if we are thrown out of his favour, our case is miserable though we dwell in our own land. This threatening, that God would make this house like Shiloh, we shall meet with again, and find Jeremiah indicted for it, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.6">ch. xxvi. 6</reference>.
entries.d46d193072212f58a568bdfd2924492cb87e4d72: <div eID="gen17334" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Punishment Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17335" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Therefore pray not thou for this people, neither lift up cry nor prayer for them, neither make intercession to me: for I will not hear thee. <hi type="super">17</hi> Seest thou not what they do in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? <hi type="super">18</hi> The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead <hi type="italic">their</hi> dough, to make cakes to the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto other gods, that they may provoke me to anger. <hi type="super">19</hi> Do they provoke me to anger? saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="italic">do they</hi> not <hi type="italic">provoke</hi> themselves to the confusion of their own faces? <hi type="super">20</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, mine anger and my fury shall be poured out upon this place, upon man, and upon beast, and upon the trees of the field, and upon the fruit of the ground; and it shall burn, and shall not be quenched. <div eID="gen17335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17336" type="x-p"/> God had shown them, in the foregoing verses, that the temple and the service of it, of which they boasted and in which they trusted, should not avail to prevent the judgment threatened. But there was another thing which might stand them in some stead, and which yet they had no value for, and that was the prophet's intercession for them; his prayers would do them more good than their own pleas: now here that support is taken from them; and their case is said indeed who have lost their interest in the prayers of God's ministers and people. <div eID="gen17336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17337" type="x-p"/> I. God here forbids the prophet to pray for them (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">v. 16</reference>): "The decree has gone forth, their ruin is resolved on, therefore <hi type="italic">pray not thou for this people,</hi> that is, pray not for the preventing of this judgment threatened; they have <hi type="italic">sinned unto death,</hi> and therefore pray not for their life, but for the life of their souls," <reference osisRef="1John.5.16">1 John v. 16</reference>. See here, 1. That God's prophets are praying men; Jeremiah foretold the destruction of Judah and Jerusalem, and yet prayed for their preservation, not knowing that the decree was absolute; and it is the will of God that we <hi type="italic">pray for the peace of Jerusalem.</hi> Even when we threaten sinners with damnation we must pray for their salvation, that they may <hi type="italic">turn and live.</hi> Jeremiah was hated, and persecuted, and reproached, by the children of his people, and yet he prayed for them; for it becomes us to render good for evil. 2. That God's praying prophets have a great interest in heaven, how little soever they have on earth. When God has determined to destroy this people, he bespeaks the prophet not to pray for them, because he would not have his prayers to lie (as prophets' prayers seldom did) unanswered. God said to Moses, <hi type="italic">Let me alone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.22.10">Exod. xxii. 10</reference>. 3. It is an ill omen to a people when God restrains the spirits of his ministers and people from praying for them, and gives them to see their case so desperate that they have no heart to speak a good word for them. 4. Those that will not regard good ministers' preaching cannot expect any benefit by their praying. If you will not hear us when we speak from God to you, God will not hear us when we speak to him for you. <div eID="gen17337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17338" type="x-p"/> II. He gives him a reason for this prohibition. Praying breath is too precious a thing to be lost and thrown away upon a people hardened in sin and marked for ruin. <div eID="gen17338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17339" type="x-p"/> 1. They are resolved to persist in their rebellion against God, and will not be turned back by the prophet's preaching. For this he appeals to the prophet himself, and his own inspection and observation (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Seest thou not what they do</hi> openly and publicly, without either shame or fear, <hi type="italic">in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?</hi> This intimates both that the sin was evident and could not be denied and that the sinners were impudent and would not be reclaimed; they committed their wickedness even in the prophet's presence and under his eye; he saw what they did, and yet they did it, which was an affront to his office, and to him whose officer he was, and bade defiance to both. Now observe, <div eID="gen17339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17340" type="x-p"/> (1.) What the sin is with which they are here charged—it is idolatry, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">v. 18</reference>. Their idolatrous respects are paid to the <hi type="italic">queen of heaven,</hi> the moon, either in an image or in the original, or both. They worshipped it probably under the name of <hi type="italic">Ashtaroth,</hi> or some other of their goddesses, being in love with the brightness in which they saw the moon walk, and thinking themselves indebted to her for her benign influences or fearing her malignant ones, <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job xxxi. 26</reference>. The worshipping of the moon was much in use among the heathen nations, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">ch. xliv. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.19">19</reference>. Some read it the <hi type="italic">frame</hi> or <hi type="italic">workmanship of heaven.</hi> The whole celestial globe with all its ornaments and powers was the object of their adoration. They <hi type="italic">worshipped the host of heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.7.42">Acts vii. 42</reference>. The homage they should have paid to their Prince they paid to the statues that beautified the frontispiece of his palace; they worshipped the creatures instead of him that made them, the servants instead of him that commands them, and the gifts instead of him that gave them. <hi type="italic">With the queen of heaven</hi> they worshipped <hi type="italic">other gods,</hi> images of things not only in <hi type="italic">heaven above, but in earth beneath, and in the waters under the earth;</hi> for those that forsake the true God wander endlessly after false ones. To these deities of their own making they offer <hi type="italic">cakes</hi> for meat-offerings, and <hi type="italic">pour out drink-offerings,</hi> as if they had their meat and drink from them and were obliged to make to them their acknowledgments: and see how busy they are, and how every hand is employed in the service of these idols, according as they used to be employed in their domestic services. <hi type="italic">The children</hi> were sent to <hi type="italic">gather wood; the fathers kindled the fire</hi> to heat the oven, being of the poorer sort that could not afford to keep servants to do it, yet they would rather do it themselves than it should be undone; <hi type="italic">the women kneaded the dough</hi> with their own hands, for perhaps, though they had servants to do it, they took a pride in showing their zeal for their idols by doing it themselves. Let us be instructed, even by this bad example, in the service of our God. [1.] Let us <hi type="italic">honour him with our substance,</hi> as those that have our subsistence from him, and eat and drink to the glory of him from whom we have our meat and drink. [2.] Let us not decline the hardest services, nor disdain to stoop to the meanest, by which God may be honoured; for none shall <hi type="italic">kindle a fire on God's altar for nought.</hi> Let us think it an honour to be employed in any work for God. [3.] Let us bring up our children in the acts of devotion; let them, as they are capable, be employed in doing something towards the keeping up of religious exercises. <div eID="gen17340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17341" type="x-p"/> (2.) What is the direct tendency of this sin: "It is <hi type="italic">that they may provoke me to anger;</hi> they cannot design any thing else in it. But (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.19">v. 19</reference>) <hi type="italic">do they provoke me to anger?</hi> Is it because I am hard to be pleased, or easily provoked? Or am I to bear the blame of the resentment? No; it is their own doing; they may thank themselves, and they alone shall bear it." <hi type="italic">Is it against God that they provoke him to wrath?</hi> Is he the worse for it? Does it do him any real damage? No; is <hi type="italic">it not against themselves,</hi> to the <hi type="italic">confusion of their own faces?</hi> It is malice against God, but it is impotent malice; it cannot hurt him: nay, it is foolish malice; it will hurt themselves. They show their spite against God, but they do the spite to themselves. Canst thou think any other than that a people, thus desperately set upon their own ruin, should be abandoned? <div eID="gen17341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17342" type="x-p"/> 2. God is resolved to proceed in his judgments against them, and will not be turned back by the prophet's prayers (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord God,</hi> and what he saith he will not unsay, nor can all the world gainsay it; hear it therefore, and tremble. "<hi type="italic">Behold, my anger and my fury shall be poured out upon this place,</hi> as the flood of waters was upon the old world or the shower of fire and brimstone upon Sodom; since they will anger me, let them see what will come of it." They shall soon find, (1.) That there is no escaping this deluge of fire, either by flying from it or fencing against it; it shall be poured out on <hi type="italic">this place,</hi> though it be a holy place, the Lord's house. It shall reach both <hi type="italic">man and beast,</hi> like the plagues of Egypt, and, like some of them, shall destroy the <hi type="italic">trees of the field and the fruit of the ground,</hi> which they had designed and <hi type="italic">prepared for Baal,</hi> and of which they had made <hi type="italic">cakes to the queen of heaven.</hi> (2.) There is no extinguishing it: <hi type="italic">It shall burn and shall not be quenched;</hi> prayers and tears shall then avail nothing. When <hi type="italic">his wrath is kindled but a little,</hi> much more when it is kindled to such a degree, there shall be no quenching it. God's wrath is that fire unquenchable which eternity itself will not see the period of. <hi type="italic">Depart, you cursed, into everlasting fire.</hi>
entries.018031cd9ab79d38ef2dd26533659c210da7bbda: <div eID="gen17342" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Obedience Better than Sacrifice. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17343" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Put your burnt offerings unto your sacrifices, and eat flesh. <hi type="super">22</hi> For I spake not unto your fathers, nor commanded them in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices: <hi type="super">23</hi> But this thing commanded I them, saying, Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and ye shall be my people: and walk ye in all the ways that I have commanded you, that it may be well unto you. <hi type="super">24</hi> But they hearkened not, nor inclined their ear, but walked in the counsels <hi type="italic">and</hi> in the imagination of their evil heart, and went backward, and not forward. <hi type="super">25</hi> Since the day that your fathers came forth out of the land of Egypt unto this day I have even sent unto you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending <hi type="italic">them:</hi> <hi type="super">26</hi> Yet they hearkened not unto me, nor inclined their ear, but hardened their neck: they did worse than their fathers. <hi type="super">27</hi> Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee: thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee. <hi type="super">28</hi> But thou shalt say unto them, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> a nation that obeyeth not the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God, nor receiveth correction: truth is perished, and is cut off from their mouth. <div eID="gen17343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17344" type="x-p"/> God, having shown the people that the temple would not protect them while they polluted it with their wickedness, here shows them that their sacrifices would not atone for them, nor be accepted, while they went on in disobedience. See with what contempt he here speaks of their ceremonial service (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.21">v. 21</reference>). "<hi type="italic">Put your burnt-offerings to your sacrifices;</hi> go on in them as long as you please; add one sort of sacrifice to another; turn your <hi type="italic">burnt-offerings</hi> (which were to be wholly burnt to the honour of God) into <hi type="italic">peace-offerings</hi>" (which the offerer himself had a considerable share of), "that you may <hi type="italic">eat flesh,</hi> for that is all the good you are likely to have from your sacrifices, a good meal's meat or two; but expect not any other benefit by them while you live at this loose rate. <hi type="italic">Keep your sacrifices to yourselves</hi>" (so some understand it); "let them be served up at your own table, for they are no way acceptable at God's altars." For the opening of this, <div eID="gen17344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17345" type="x-p"/> I. He shows them that obedience was the only thing he required of them, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.22-Jer.7.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. He appeals to the original contract, by which they were first formed into a people, when they were brought out of Egypt. God made them a <hi type="italic">kingdom of priests</hi> to himself, not that he might be regaled with their sacrifices, as the devils, whom the heathen worshipped, which are represented as eating with pleasure the fat of their sacrifices and drinking the wine of their drink-offerings, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.38">Deut. xxxii. 38</reference>. No: <hi type="italic">Will God eat the flesh of bulls?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.13">Ps. l. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">I spoke not to your fathers concerning burnt-offerings or sacrifices,</hi> not of them <hi type="italic">at first.</hi> The precepts of the moral law were given before the ceremonial institutions; and those came afterwards, as trials of their obedience and assistances to their repentance and faith. The Levitical law begins thus: <hi type="italic">If any man of you will bring an offering,</hi> he must do so and so (<reference osisRef="Lev.1.2">Lev. i. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.2.1">ii. 1</reference>), as if it were intended rather to regulate sacrifice than to require it. But that which God commanded, which he bound them to by his supreme authority and which he insisted upon as the condition of the covenant, was, <hi type="italic">Obey my voice;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Exod.15.26">Exod. xv. 26</reference>, where this was the statute and the ordinance by which God proved them: <hi type="italic">Hearken diligently to the voice of the Lord thy God.</hi> The condition of their being God's peculiar people was this (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Exod. xix. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">If you will obey my voice indeed.</hi> "Make conscience of the duties of natural religion, observe positive institutions from a principle of obedience, and then <hi type="italic">I will be your God and you shall be my people,</hi>" which is the greatest honour, happiness, and satisfaction, that any of the children of men are capable of. "Let your conversation be regular, and in every thing study to comply with the will and word of God; <hi type="italic">walk</hi> within the bounds that I have set you, and <hi type="italic">in all the ways that I have commanded you,</hi> and then you may assure yourselves that <hi type="italic">it shall be well with you.</hi>" The demand here is very reasonable, that we should be directed by Infinite Wisdom to that which is fit, that he that made us should command us, and that he should give us law who gives us our being and all the supports of it; and the promise is very encouraging: Let God's will be your rule and his favour shall be your felicity. <div eID="gen17345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17346" type="x-p"/> II. He shows them that disobedience was the only thing for which he had a quarrel with them. <hi type="italic">He would not reprove them for their sacrifices,</hi> for the omission of them; they had been <hi type="italic">continually before him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">Ps. l. 8</reference>); with them they hoped to bribe God, and purchase a license to go on in sin. That therefore which God had all along laid to their charge was breaking his commandments in the course of their conversation, while they observed them, in some instances, in the course of their devotion, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.24-Jer.7.25">v. 24, 25</reference>, &c. 1. They set up their own will in competition with the will of God: <hi type="italic">They hearkened not</hi> to God and to his law; they never heeded that; it was to them as if it had never been given or were of no force; they <hi type="italic">inclined not their ear</hi> to attend to it, much less their hearts to comply with it. But they would have their own way, would do as they chose, and not as they were bidden. <hi type="italic">Their own counsels</hi> were their guide, and not the dictates of divine wisdom; that shall be lawful and good with them which they think so, though the word of God says quite contrary. <hi type="italic">The imagination of their evil heart,</hi> the appetites and passions of it, shall be a law to them, and they will walk in the way of it, and in the sight of their eyes. 2. If they began well, yet they did not proceed, but soon flew off. They <hi type="italic">went backward,</hi> when they talked of making a captain, and returning to Egypt again, and would not go forward under God's conduct. They promised fair: <hi type="italic">All that the Lord shall say unto us we will do;</hi> and, if they would but have kept in that good mind, all would have been well; but, instead of going on in the way of duty, they drew back into the way of sin, and were worse than ever. 3. When God sent to them by word of mouth to put them in mind of the written word, which was the business of the prophets, it was all one; still they were disobedient. God had servants of his among them in every age, <hi type="italic">since they came out of Egypt unto this day,</hi> some or other to tell them of their faults and put them in mind of their duty, whom he <hi type="italic">rose up early to send</hi> (as before, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.13">v. 13</reference>), as men rise up early to call servants to their work; but they were as deaf to the prophets as they were to the law (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet they hearkened not, nor inclined their ear.</hi> This had been their way and manner all along; they were of the same stubborn refractory disposition with those that went before them; it had all along been the genius of the nation, and an evil genius it was, that continually haunted them till it ruined them at last. 4. Their practice and character were still the same. They are worse, and not better, <hi type="italic">than their fathers.</hi> (1.) Jeremiah can himself witness against them that they were disobedient, or he shall soon find it so (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.27">v. 27</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt speak all these words to them,</hi> shalt particularly charge them with disobedience and obstinacy. But even that will not work upon them: <hi type="italic">They will not hearken to thee,</hi> nor heed thee. Thou shalt go, and <hi type="italic">call to them</hi> with all the plainness and earnestness imaginable, but <hi type="italic">they will not answer thee;</hi> they will either give thee no answer at all or not an obedient answer; they will not come at thy call." (2.) He must therefore own that they deserved the character of a disobedient people, that were ripe for destruction, and must go to them and tell them so to their faces (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.28">v. 28</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Say unto them, This is a nation that obeys not the voice of the Lord their God.</hi> They are notorious for their obstinacy; they sacrifice to the Lord as their God, but they will not be ruled by him as their God; they will not receive either the instruction of his word or the correction of his rod; they will not be reclaimed or reformed by either. <hi type="italic">Truth has perished</hi> among them; they cannot receive it; they will not submit to it nor be governed by it. They will not speak truth; there is no believing a word they say, for it is <hi type="italic">cut off from their mouth,</hi> and lying comes in the room of it. They are false both to God and man."
entries.dadeaab88ff1f7c661f2fa718c4b26ee8461ba88: <div eID="gen17346" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Desolation of Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17347" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> Cut off thine hair, <hi type="italic">O Jerusalem,</hi> and cast <hi type="italic">it</hi> away, and take up a lamentation on high places; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath. <hi type="super">30</hi> For the children of Judah have done evil in my sight, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : they have set their abominations in the house which is called by my name, to pollute it. <hi type="super">31</hi> And they have built the high places of Tophet, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I commanded <hi type="italic">them</hi> not, neither came it into my heart. <hi type="super">32</hi> Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that it shall no more be called Tophet, nor the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter: for they shall bury in Tophet, till there be no place. <hi type="super">33</hi> And the carcases of this people shall be meat for the fowls of the heaven, and for the beasts of the earth; and none shall fray <hi type="italic">them</hi> away. <hi type="super">34</hi> Then will I cause to cease from the cities of Judah, and from the streets of Jerusalem, the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride: for the land shall be desolate. <div eID="gen17347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17348" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A loud call to weeping and mourning. Jerusalem, that had been a joyous city, the joy of the whole earth, must now <hi type="italic">take up a lamentation on high places</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.29">v. 29</reference>), the high places where they had served their idols; there must they now bemoan their misery. In token both of sorrow and slavery, Jerusalem must now <hi type="italic">cut off her hair and cast it away;</hi> the word is peculiar to the hair of the Nazarites, which was the badge and token of their dedication to God, and it is called <hi type="italic">their crown.</hi> Jerusalem had been a city which was a Nazarite to God, but now must <hi type="italic">cut off her hair,</hi> must be profaned, degraded, and separated from God, as she had been separated to him. It is time for those that have lost their holiness to lay aside their joy. <div eID="gen17348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17349" type="x-p"/> II. Just cause given for this great lamentation. <div eID="gen17349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17350" type="x-p"/> 1. The sin of Jerusalem appears here very heinous, nowhere worse, or more exceedingly sinful (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.30">v. 30</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The children of Judah</hi>" (God's profession people, that <hi type="italic">came forth out of the waters of Judah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.1">Isa. xlviii. 1</reference>) "<hi type="italic">have done evil in my sight,</hi> under my eye, in my presence; they have affronted me to my face, which very much aggravates the affront:" or, "They have done that which they know to be <hi type="italic">evil in my sight,</hi> and in the highest degree offensive to me." Idolatry was the sin which was above all other sins evil in God's sight. Now here are two things charged upon them in their idolatry, which were very provoking: (1.) That they were very impudent in it towards God and set him at defiance: <hi type="italic">They have set their abominations</hi> (their abominable idols and the altars erected to them) <hi type="italic">in the house that is called by my name,</hi> in the very courts of the temple, <hi type="italic">to pollute it</hi> (Manasseh did so, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.7">2 Kings xxi. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.12">xxiii. 12</reference>), as if they thought God would connive at it, or cared not though he was ever so much displeased with it, or as if they would reconcile heaven and hell, God and Baal. The heart is the place which God has chosen to <hi type="italic">put his name there;</hi> if sin have the innermost and uppermost place there, we pollute the temple of the Lord, and therefore he resents nothing more than <hi type="italic">setting up idols in the heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.4">Ezek. xiv. 4</reference>. (2.) That they were very barbarous in it towards their own children, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.31">v. 31</reference>. They have particularly <hi type="italic">built the high places of Tophet,</hi> where the image of Moloch was set up, <hi type="italic">in the valley of the son of Hinnom,</hi> adjoining to Jerusalem; and there <hi type="italic">they burnt their sons and their daughters in the fire,</hi> burnt them alive, killed them, and killed them in the most cruel manner imaginable, to honour or appease those idols that were devils and not gods. This was surely the greatest instance that ever was of the power of Satan in the children of disobedience, and of the degeneracy and corruption of the human nature. One would willingly hope that there were not many instances of such a barbarous idolatry; but it is amazing that there should be any, that men could be so perfectly void of natural affection as to do a thing so inhuman as to burn little innocent children, and their own too, that they should be so perfectly void of natural religion as to think it lawful to do this, nay, to think it acceptable. Surely it was in a way of righteous judgment, because they had changed the glory of God into the similitude of a beast, that God gave them up to such vile affections that changed them into worse than beasts. God says of this that it was <hi type="italic">what he commanded them not, neither came it into his heart,</hi> which is not meant of his not commanding them thus to worship Moloch (this he had expressly <hi type="italic">forbidden</hi> them), but he had never commanded that his worshippers should be at such an expense, nor put such a force upon their natural affection, in honouring him; it never came into his heart to have children offered to him, yet they had forsaken his service for the service of such gods as, by commanding this, showed themselves to be indeed enemies to mankind. <div eID="gen17350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17351" type="x-p"/> 2. The destruction of Jerusalem appears here very terrible. That speaks misery enough in general (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.29">v. 29</reference>), <hi type="italic">The Lord hath rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath.</hi> Sin makes those the generation of God's wrath that had been the generation of his love. And God will reject and quite forsake those who have thus made themselves <hi type="italic">vessels of wrath fitted to destruction.</hi> He will disown them for his. "Verily, I say unto you, I know you not." And he will give them up to the terrors of their own guilt, and leave them in those hands. (1.) Death shall triumph over them, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.32-Jer.7.33">v. 32, 33</reference>. Sin reigns unto death; for that is the wages of it, the end of those things. <hi type="italic">Tophet,</hi> the valley adjoining to Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">shall be called the valley of slaughter,</hi> for there multitudes shall be slain, when, in their sallies out of the city and their attempts to escape, they fall into the hands of the besiegers. Or it shall be called <hi type="italic">the valley of slaughtered ones,</hi> because thither the corpses of those that are slain shall be brought to be buried, all other burying places being full; and there they shall bury <hi type="italic">until there be no more place</hi> to make a grave. This intimates the multitude of those that shall die by the sword, pestilence, and famine. Death shall ride on prosperously, with dreadful pomp and power, <hi type="italic">conquering and to conquer. The slain of the Lord shall be many.</hi> This valley of Tophet was a place where the citizens of Jerusalem walked to take the air; but it shall now be spoiled for that use, for it shall be so full of graves that there shall be no walking there, because of the danger of contracting a ceremonial pollution by the touch of a grave. There it was that they sacrificed some of their children, and dedicated others to Moloch, and there they should fall as victims to divine justice. Tophet had formerly been the burying place, or burning place, of the dead bodies of the besiegers, when the Assyrian army was routed by an angel; and for this it was <hi type="italic">ordained of old,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa. xxx. 33</reference>. But they having forgotten this mercy, and made it the place of their sin, God will now turn it into a burying place for the besieged. In allusion to this valley, hell is in the New Testament called <hi type="italic">Gehenna—the valley of Hinnom,</hi> for there were buried both the invading Assyrians and the revolting Jews; so hell is a receptacle after death both for infidels and hypocrites, the open enemies of God's church and its treacherous friends; it is <hi type="italic">the congregation of the dead;</hi> it is prepared for the <hi type="italic">generation of God's wrath.</hi> But so great shall that slaughter be that even the spacious valley of Tophet shall not be able to contain the slain; and at length there shall not be enough left alive to bury the dead, so that <hi type="italic">the carcases of the people shall be meat</hi> for the birds and beasts of prey, that shall feed upon them like carrion, and none shall have the concern or courage to frighten them away, as Rizpah did from the dead bodies of Saul's sons, <reference osisRef="2Sam.28.26">2 Sam. xxviii. 26</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thy carcase shall be meat to the fowls and beasts, and no man shall drive them away.</hi> Thus do the law and the prophets agree, and the execution with both. The decent burying of the dead is a piece of humanity, in remembrance of what the dead body has been—the tabernacle of a reasonable soul. Nay, it is a piece of divinity, in expectation of what the dead body shall be at the resurrection. The want of it has sometimes been an instance of the rage of men against God's witnesses, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.9">Rev. xi. 9</reference>. Here it is threatened as an instance of the wrath of God against his enemies, and is an intimation that <hi type="italic">evil pursues sinners</hi> even after death. (2.) Joy shall depart from them (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then will I cause to cease the voice of mirth.</hi> God had <hi type="italic">called</hi> by his prophets, and by less judgments, <hi type="italic">to weeping and mourning;</hi> but they walked contrary to him, and would hear of nothing but joy and gladness, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.12-Isa.22.13">Isa. xxii. 12, 13</reference>. And what came of it? Now God <hi type="italic">called to lamentation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.29">v. 29</reference>), and he made his call effectual, leaving them neither cause nor heart for joy and gladness. Those that will not weep shall weep; those that will not by the grace of God be cured of their vain mirth shall by the justice of God be deprived of all mirth; for <hi type="italic">when God judges he will overcome.</hi> It is threatened here that there shall be nothing to rejoice in. There shall be none of the joy of weddings; no mirth, for there shall be no marriages. The comforts of life shall be abandoned, and all care to keep up mankind upon earth cast off; there shall be none of <hi type="italic">the voice of the bridegroom and</hi> the <hi type="italic">bride,</hi> no music, no nuptial songs. Nor shall there be any more of the joy of the harvest, <hi type="italic">for the land shall be desolate,</hi> uncultivated and unimproved. Both <hi type="italic">the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem</hi> shall look thus melancholy; and when they thus look about them, and see no cause to rejoice, no marvel if they retire into themselves and find no heart to rejoice. Note, God can soon mar the mirth of the most jovial, and make it to cease, which is a reason why we should always rejoice with trembling, be merry and wise.  <chapter eID="Jer.7"/> <div eID="gen17351" type="x-p"/>

entries.a76d927aed7f912f15366a049897d12e5376a267: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9741"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.7.1-Jer.7.34">Jr 7:1-34</reference>. The Seventh through Ninth Chapters. Delivered in the Beginning of Jehoiakim's Reign, on the Occasion of Some Public Festival.</title> <div sID="gen17215" type="x-p"/> The prophet stood at the gate of the temple in order that the multitudes from the country might hear him. His life was threatened, it appears from <reference osisRef="Jer.26.1-Jer.26.9">Jr 26:1-9</reference>, for this prophecy, denouncing the fate of Shiloh as about to befall the temple at Jerusalem. The prophecy given in detail here is summarily referred to there. After Josiah's death the nation relapsed into idolatry through Jehoiakim's bad influence; the worship of Jehovah was, however, combined with it (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jr 7:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen17215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17216" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9741"/><hi type="bold">2. the gate--</hi>that is, the gate of the court of Israel within that of the women. Those whom Jeremiah addresses came through the gate leading into the court of the women, and the gate leading into the outer court, or court of the Gentiles ("these gates"). <div eID="gen17216" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d267bf386885fb16bc1718212e2def3da4df232: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9742"/><div sID="gen17217" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9742"/><hi type="bold">3. cause you to dwell--</hi>permit you still to dwell (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.11">Jr 18:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.26.13">26:13</reference>). <div eID="gen17217" type="x-p"/>
entries.04d3fd58994bc3727e8268a3b647b490a86c3c88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9743"/><div sID="gen17218" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9743"/>4. The Jews falsely thought that because their temple had been chosen by Jehovah as His peculiar dwelling, it could never be destroyed. Men think that ceremonial observances will supersede the need of holiness (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.2">Is 48:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mi 3:11</reference>). The triple repetition of "the temple of Jehovah" expresses the intense confidence of the Jews (see <reference osisRef="Jer.22.29">Jr 22:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Is 6:3</reference>).<div eID="gen17218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">these--</hi>the temple buildings which the prophet points to with his finger (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.2">Jr 7:2</reference>). <div eID="gen17219" type="x-p"/>

For--</hi>"But" [Maurer].<div eID="gen17220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment--</hi>justice (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.3">Jr 22:3</reference>). <div eID="gen17221" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a8c489678319437f93b6d0575b79574f83be78f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9745"/><div sID="gen17222" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9745"/><hi type="bold">6. this place--</hi>this city and land (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.7">Jr 7:7</reference>).<div eID="gen17222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to your hurt--</hi>so <reference osisRef="Jer.7.19">Jr 7:19</reference>; "to the confusion or their own faces" (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.10">Jr 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.36">Pr 8:36</reference>). <div eID="gen17223" type="x-p"/>

entries.b7f2e44a5e7d00e3d9e25f191f3c431a911ba027: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9747"/><div sID="gen17227" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9747"/><hi type="bold">8. that cannot profit--</hi>Maurer translates, "so that you profit nothing" (see <reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jr 7:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">Jr 5:31</reference>). <div eID="gen17227" type="x-p"/>
entries.b48b12181ae5422aaffc220d939b951eba03d49a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9748"/><div sID="gen17228" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9748"/>9-10. "Will ye steal ... and then come and stand before Me?"<div eID="gen17228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whom ye know not--</hi>Ye have no grounds of "knowing" that they are gods; but I have manifested My Godhead by My law, by benefits conferred, and by miracles. This aggravates their crime [Calvin] (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.8">Jud 5:8</reference>). <div eID="gen17229" type="x-p"/>
entries.da15324f200422bd56d9f7f48d70db073b2fce14: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9750"/><div sID="gen17233" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9750"/><hi type="bold">11. den of robbers--</hi>Do you regard My temple as being what robbers make their den, namely, an asylum wherein ye may obtain impunity for your abominations (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.10">Jr 7:10</reference>)?<div eID="gen17233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17234" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seen it--</hi>namely, that ye treat My house as if it were a den of thieves. Jehovah implies more than is expressed, "I have seen and will punish it" (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.7">Is 56:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.13">Mt 21:13</reference>). <div eID="gen17234" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d64d066beab2711312ca234ae73d9e5dc12600e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9751"/><div sID="gen17235" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9751"/><hi type="bold">12. my place ... in Shiloh--</hi>God caused His tabernacle to be set up in Shiloh in Joshua's days (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.1">Jos 18:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.18.31">Jud 18:31</reference>). In Eli's time God gave the ark, which had been at Shiloh, into the hands of the Philistines (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.6">Jr 26:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.10">1Sa 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.56-Ps.78.61">Psa 78:56-61</reference>). Shiloh was situated between Beth-el and Shechem in Ephraim.<div eID="gen17235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17236" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at the first--</hi>implying that Shiloh exceeded the Jewish temple in antiquity. But God's favor is not tied down to localities (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.44">Ac 7:44</reference>).<div eID="gen17236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my people Israel--</hi>Israel was God's people, yet He spared it not when rebellious: neither will He spare Judah, now that it rebels, though heretofore it has been His people. <div eID="gen17237" type="x-p"/>
entries.0dc626330f939cc82b73296b182a1abb8c0646f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9752"/><div sID="gen17238" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9752"/><hi type="bold">13. rising ... early--</hi>implying unwearied earnestness in soliciting them (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.25">Jr 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.11.17">Jr 11:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.15">2Ch 36:15</reference>). <div eID="gen17238" type="x-p"/>
entries.53e58b934f01eccc26e4fa0114a9b890b7fd4a0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9753"/><div sID="gen17239" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9753"/><hi type="bold">14. I gave--</hi>and I therefore can revoke the gift for it is still Mine (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.23">Le 25:23</reference>), now that ye fail in the only object for which it was given, the promotion of My glory.<div eID="gen17239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shiloh--</hi>as I ceased to dwell there, transferring My temple to Jerusalem; so I will cease to dwell at Jerusalem. <div eID="gen17240" type="x-p"/>
entries.822a83e8a4932521b760d6a0a86ced93e24594b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9754"/><div sID="gen17241" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9754"/><hi type="bold">15. your brethren--</hi>children of Abraham, as much as you.<div eID="gen17241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whole seed of Ephraim--</hi>They were superior to you in numbers and power: they were ten tribes: ye but two. "Ephraim," as the leading tribe, stands for the whole ten tribes (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.23">2Ki 17:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.67">Psa 78:67</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.68">68</reference>). <div eID="gen17242" type="x-p"/>
entries.05e43bff817b344b5bcb146cacb3052e01b4a82b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9755"/><div sID="gen17243" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9755"/>16. When people are given up to judicial hardness of heart, intercessory prayer for them is unavailing (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.14">Jr 11:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.11">14:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.1">15:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.10">Ex 32:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.16">1Jo 5:16</reference>). <div eID="gen17243" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1430c487a998e0662ae273113ddc9c7c0b2f0b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9756"/><div sID="gen17244" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9756"/>17. Jehovah leaves it to Jeremiah himself to decide, is there not good reason that prayers should not be heard in behalf of such rebels? <div eID="gen17244" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd2b622e8187f1d80456dd672e61a78090167cef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9757"/><div sID="gen17245" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9757"/><hi type="bold">18. children ... fathers ... women--</hi>Not merely isolated individuals practised idolatry; young and old, men and women, and whole families, contributed their joint efforts to promote it. Oh, that there were the same zeal for the worship of God as there is for error (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">Jr 44:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.19.13">19:13</reference>)!<div eID="gen17245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cakes ... queen of heaven--</hi>Cakes were made of honey, fine flour, &c., in a round flat shape to resemble the disc of the moon, to which they were offered. Others read as Margin, "the frame of heaven," that is, the planets generally; so the Septuagint here; but elsewhere the Septuagint translates, "queen of heaven." The Phoenicians called the moon Ashtoreth or Astarte: the wife of Baal or Moloch, the king of heaven. The male and female pair of deities symbolized the generative powers of nature; hence arose the introduction of prostitution in the worship. The Babylonians worshipped Ashtoreth as Mylitta, that is, generative. Our Monday, or Moon-day, indicates the former prevalence of moon worship (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.65.11">Is 65:11</reference>).<div eID="gen17246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they may provoke me--</hi>implying design: in worshipping strange gods they seemed as if purposely to provoke Jehovah. <div eID="gen17247" type="x-p"/>
entries.d33d8b51c2082b625848e7d54709a4ffe011ccd1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9758"/><div sID="gen17248" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9758"/>19. Is it I that they provoke to anger? Is it not themselves? (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.16">De 32:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.35.6">Job 35:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.35.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.36">Pr 8:36</reference>). <div eID="gen17248" type="x-p"/>
entries.48d3e2e5a9103433035128771567d7dd59385064: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9759"/><div sID="gen17249" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9759"/><hi type="bold">20. beast ... trees ... ground--</hi>Why doth God vent His fury on these? On account of man, for whom these were created, that the sad spectacle may strike terror into him (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.20-Rom.8.22">Ro 8:20-22</reference>). <div eID="gen17249" type="x-p"/>
entries.d69cd55852d8f3ed366a7f3e378cb953341b8ea5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9760"/><div sID="gen17250" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9760"/><hi type="bold">21. Put ... burnt offerings unto ... sacrifices ... eat flesh--</hi>Add the former (which the law required to be wholly burnt) to the latter (which were burnt only in part), and "eat flesh" even off the holocausts or burnt offerings. As far as I am concerned, saith Jehovah, you may do with one and the other alike. I will have neither (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Is 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.13">Ho 8:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.21">Am 5:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.22">22</reference>). <div eID="gen17250" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf3e0083262e6c02829889af7c79b848e449640c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9761"/><div sID="gen17251" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9761"/>22. Not contradicting the divine obligation of the legal sacrifices. But, "I did not require sacrifices, unless combined with moral obedience" (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">Psa 50:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.16">51:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.17">17</reference>). The superior claim of the moral above the positive precepts of the law was marked by the ten commandments having been delivered first, and by the two tables of stone being deposited alone in the ark (<reference osisRef="Deut.5.6">De 5:6</reference>). The negative in Hebrew often supplies the want of the comparative: not excluding the thing denied, but only implying the prior claim of the thing set in opposition to it (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">Ho 6:6</reference>). "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>). Love to God is the supreme end, external observances only means towards that end. "The mere sacrifice was not so much what I commanded, as the sincere submission to My will gives to the sacrifice all its virtue" [Magee, Atonement, Note 57]. <div eID="gen17251" type="x-p"/>

(<reference osisRef="Exod.15.26">Ex 15:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">19:5</reference>). <div eID="gen17252" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf1bd06d4195cc096203ca872f784497b23dcdac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9763"/><div sID="gen17253" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9763"/><hi type="bold">24. hearkened not--</hi>They did not give even a partial hearing to Me (<reference osisRef="Ps.81.11">Psa 81:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.81.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen17253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17254" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">imagination--</hi>rather, as Margin, "the stubbornness."<div eID="gen17254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17255" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">backward, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.2.27">Jr 2:27</reference>; 32:33; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.16">Ho 4:16</reference>). <div eID="gen17255" type="x-p"/>
entries.af237944f2fd772d1d32feeb629de399919ce8bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9764"/><div sID="gen17256" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9764"/><hi type="bold">25. rising ... early--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.7.13">Jr 7:13</reference>). <div eID="gen17256" type="x-p"/>
entries.04d70dc11b1fb569621ddc50095c4e1677a10451: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9765"/><div sID="gen17257" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9765"/><hi type="bold">26. hardened ... neck--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.31.27">De 31:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.4">Is 48:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.51">Ac 7:51</reference>).<div eID="gen17257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worse than their fathers--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.16.12">Jr 16:12</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Jer.7.22">Jr 7:22</reference> He had said, "your fathers"; here He says, "their fathers"; the change to the third person marks growing alienation from them. He no longer addresses themselves, as it would be a waste of words in the case of such hardened rebels. <div eID="gen17258" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac653b1e7eaa8681dec138e8edb8226c0a52aeae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9766"/><div sID="gen17259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9766"/><hi type="bold">27. Therefore--</hi>rather, "Though thou speak ... yet they will not hearken" [Maurer], (<reference osisRef="Ezek.2.7">Eze 2:7</reference>), a trial to the prophet's faith; though he knew his warnings would be unheeded, still he was to give them in obedience to God. <div eID="gen17259" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b88a570b7a0e979485b680c34b906f973d6c736: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9767"/><div sID="gen17260" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9767"/><hi type="bold">28. unto them--</hi>that is, in reference to them.<div eID="gen17260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a nation--</hi>The word usually applied to the Gentile nations is here applied to the Jews, as being east off and classed by God among the Gentiles.<div eID="gen17261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor receiveth correction--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.5.3">Jr 5:3</reference>).<div eID="gen17262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">truth ... perished--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.9.3">Jr 9:3</reference>). <div eID="gen17263" type="x-p"/>
entries.44672d3ffa8064d4a1bcb85bcd9cb846444c01ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9768"/><div sID="gen17264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9768"/>29. Jeremiah addresses Jerusalem under the figure of a woman, who, in grief for her lost children, deprives her head of its chief ornament and goes up to the hills to weep (<reference osisRef="Judg.11.37">Jud 11:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.38">38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.15.2">Is 15:2</reference>).<div eID="gen17264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hair--</hi>flowing locks, like those of a Nazarite.<div eID="gen17265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17266" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">high places--</hi>The scene of her idolatries is to be the scene of her mourning (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.21">Jr 3:21</reference>).<div eID="gen17266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">generation of his wrath--</hi>the generation with which He is wroth. So <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">Is 10:6</reference>; "the people of My wrath." <div eID="gen17267" type="x-p"/>
entries.73abf515eb5b70d838b5badcf2313da47ef3cc70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9769"/><div sID="gen17268" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9769"/><hi type="bold">30. set their abominations in the house--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.32.34">Jr 32:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.4">2Ki 21:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.4">23:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.5-Ezek.8.14">Eze 8:5-14</reference>). <div eID="gen17268" type="x-p"/>
entries.83696db372bddea7387665aff031aff5a4711e18: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9770"/><div sID="gen17269" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9770"/><hi type="bold">31. high places of Tophet--</hi>the altars [Horsley] of Tophet; erected to Moloch, on the heights along the south of the valley facing Zion.<div eID="gen17269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burn ... sons--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.106.38">Psa 106:38</reference>).<div eID="gen17270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17271" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commanded ... not--</hi>put for, "I forbade expressly" (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.3">De 17:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.31">12:31</reference>).
